Against a Tit-for-Tat partner, my position is always the same: they will be silent this round if and only if I was silent last round. So at every decision point, I'm facing the same local choice:

| My move this round | I get now | They do next round | I get next round |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stay silent | 1 year | Silent | 1 year |
| Talk | 0 years | Talk | 5 years |

Defecting saves me **1 year** this round but costs me **4 years** next round. Net: I lose 3 years per defection. That's the entire game, compressed.

The only round where defection is free is the last one — no punishment to come. But I never know which round that is. At any given round, I have to weigh:

- **Gain if I defect:** 1 year (immediate)
- **Cost if I defect:** 4 years × *probability the game continues*

Defection only pays off if I believe there's more than a 75% chance the game ends after this round. I have no reason to believe that about any particular round. So the expected value of defection is always negative.

## Would It Change as Things Go On?

No. And that's the elegant part.

If I always cooperate, the history is always *(silent, silent)*. There's no bad round to react to, no escalation to de-escalate, no pattern to break. My silence guarantees their silence, which makes my silence the best response, which guarantees their silence, and so on. The strategy is **self-reinforcing** — it creates the very conditions that make it optimal.

There's no "turning point" where I should start talking. No round number where the math shifts. The 3-year cost of defection is identical whether it's round 2 or round 200.

Suppose I *did* defect (hypothetically) and I'm now in the punishment state — they're talking because I talked last round. Should I talk back or absorb it?

- **Stay silent:** I take 5 this round, then 1 next round → 6 total
- **Talk back:** I take 3 this round, then 3 next round → 6 total

Over two rounds it's a wash. Over three rounds, staying silent wins (7 vs. 9). So even in the bad state, the right move is to swallow the punishment and return to silence. But again — I should never be in that state to begin with.

Tit-for-Tat turns the Prisoner's Dilemma into a game where cooperation is the unique rational strategy, *provided the future is long enough*. The "shadow of the future" — the knowledge that today's betrayal gets punished tomorrow — is doing all the work. I don't need to be generous, or principled, or even like my partner. I just need to not be short-sighted. And since I can't identify the last round, I can never safely be short-sighted.

Silence, forever.
